data.name: EveFound
data.value: Eve tries the exponents of g = {1} modulo {0} until she gets A = {2}: she finds a = {3} and then B^a = {4}, the key. With such a small prime this is quick; with 2048 bits it is not feasible.

data.name: ExchangeExplanation
data.value: Alice and Bob agree on the prime p = {0} and the generator g = {1}. Each chooses a secret exponent, sends g to the power of it, and raises what the other sent to the power of the own secret: both get g^(ab) mod p. Eve sees only p, g, A and B.

data.name: ExchangeTitle
data.value: Diffie-Hellman key exchange

data.name: ForwardSecrecyDifferent
data.value: The sessions have different keys: new exponents give a new key every time.

data.name: ForwardSecrecyExplanation
data.value: Perfect forward secrecy: the exponents a and b are used for one session only and are then deleted. Even if someone later gets the long-term keys of Alice and Bob, or records all the sessions, the old keys cannot be found, because nothing that remains determines them.

data.name: ForwardSecrecySame
data.value: Two sessions have the same key, because the exponents give the same result.

data.name: ParametersTooltip
data.value: Numbers separated by spaces. Diffie-Hellman: p g a1 b1 [a2 b2 ...] (prime, generator, secret exponents of Alice and Bob per session). Signature: p q e (two primes and the public exponent of an RSA key). Authentication: password challenge1 challenge2 (three words). S/MIME: pA qA eA pB qB eB (the RSA keys of Alice and Bob). TLS: p g a b (prime, generator, secret exponents of client and server). Zero-knowledge: p q s r1 c1 [r2 c2 ...] (two primes, the secret, and per round the random number and the challenge 0 or 1).

data.name: SignatureExplanation
data.value: Alice has the RSA key n = {0}, e = {1} (public) and d = {2} (private). She hashes the message and signs the hash value with her private key; Bob hashes the message he received and compares it with what the signature gives with Alice's public key.

data.name: SignatureInvalid
data.value: The signature is NOT valid: s^e mod n = {0}, but h' = {1}. The message is not the one Alice signed.

data.name: SignatureTitle
data.value: Digital signature

data.name: SignatureValid
data.value: The signature is valid: s^e mod n = {0} equals h'. The message is from Alice and was not changed.

data.name: SmallKeyNote
data.value: The key of the example is very small: the hash value (256 bits) is reduced modulo n, so different messages can have the same signature. Real keys have 2048 bits or more, and the whole hash value is signed (with a padding).

data.name: SmimeExplanation
data.value: Alice signs the message with her private key, encrypts message and signature with a session key (a fast symmetric cipher) and encrypts the session key with Bob's public key. Bob reverses the steps with his private key and checks the signature with Alice's public key.

data.name: SmimeInvalid
data.value: The signature is NOT valid.

data.name: SmimeNote
data.value: The RSA keys of the example are tiny, so the session key is encrypted byte by byte and the hash value is reduced modulo n. With real keys (2048 bits or more) the whole session key is encrypted in one piece, with padding, and the whole hash value is signed.

data.name: SmimeTitle
data.value: S/MIME: signed and encrypted e-mail

data.name: SmimeValid
data.value: Bob can read the message, and the signature is valid: the message is from Alice and was not changed.

data.name: TlsEveFound
data.value: Eve sees p, g, A and B and finds the exponent a = {0} by trial: she computes the same secret and all keys. With a real group this is not feasible.

data.name: TlsEveNotTried
data.value: The prime is too large for Eve to find the exponent by trial.

data.name: TlsExplanation
data.value: The client and the server exchange key shares (Diffie-Hellman), both compute the same secret, and from it, the hash of the messages and HKDF all keys follow. The Finished messages prove that both sides have the same keys and have seen the same messages. This example uses a small Diffie-Hellman group instead of an elliptic curve, and the certificate is only named.

data.name: TlsFailed
data.value: A Finished message is wrong: the handshake fails.

data.name: TlsNote
data.value: The key schedule is the one of RFC 8446 (HKDF-Extract and HKDF-Expand-Label with SHA-256); only the Diffie-Hellman group, the message encoding and the certificate are simplified. The messages after the ServerHello are encrypted with the handshake keys; the key for the data comes from the hash of all handshake messages.

data.name: TlsOk
data.value: Both Finished messages are correct: the handshake succeeded and both sides use the same application keys.

data.name: TlsTitle
data.value: TLS 1.3 handshake: how client and server agree on keys

data.name: ZkCheaterText
data.value: The cheater bets on c = 0: he sends x = r^2 and can answer only y = r. If Victor asks c = 1, the cheater would need r * s and fails.

data.name: ZkCheaterTitle
data.value: A cheater who does not know s

data.name: ZkExplanation
data.value: Peggy proves to Victor that she knows a square root s of v modulo n without revealing s. In every round she commits with x = r^2, Victor asks for r (c = 0) or for r * s (c = 1), and he checks the answer with the public values. A round that is answered correctly shows nothing about s, but a cheater is caught with probability 1/2 in each round.

data.name: ZkNote
data.value: The numbers are small so that they can be followed by hand. With a modulus of 2048 bits and 40 or more rounds the cheater has a probability below 2^-40.
